why: no model has been rendered and compared with the unit
claim: The byte a page prints `Threshold` against is decibels, 0.4776 of them a step over two independent twenty-one step stretches that agree to 0.0009, and the limiting stops at byte 61.2 for the level this was read at, above which the four states of the ratio byte are one reading to 0.01 of a decibel. The type takes a further 2.7 decibels off whatever it is doing, constant across thirty decibels of input and therefore not limiting. Of the four states of the byte printed `Ratio`, only the one printed `1/100` behaves as a ratio: its gain reduction is proportional to how far the signal sits over the threshold to a part in a thousand. The other three do not. Walked as a ladder instead -- the level going in moved thirty-six decibels at one setting of the threshold byte, which uses no part of that byte -- each of the four states returns a slope, and one minus that slope comes back 0.2499, 0.5052, 0.7518 and 0.9947: a quarter, a half, three quarters and all of the level over the threshold, to within a part in a hundred. The page names the middle two of those correctly and the outer two not. The state printed `1/1.5` takes three quarters of the level away where two thirds is printed against it, and the state printed `1/100` holds its output still to a hundredth of a decibel over eight decibels of input, where one part in a hundred would have moved it eight times the run's own floor. What the sentence before this one says of the other three is about their gain reduction being proportional to the distance over the threshold, which is a different quantity from the slope: each of them still takes six to eight and a half tenths of a decibel off where the signal sits at the threshold, so the line they follow does not pass through it. Walked as a ladder instead -- the level going in moved thirty-six decibels at one setting of the threshold byte, which uses no part of that byte -- each of the four states returns a slope, and one minus that slope comes back 0.2499, 0.5052, 0.7518 and 0.9947: a quarter, a half, three quarters and all of the level over the threshold, to within a part in a hundred. The page names the middle two of those correctly and the outer two not. The state printed `1/1.5` takes three quarters of the level away where two thirds is printed against it, and the state printed `1/100` holds its output still to a hundredth of a decibel over eight decibels of input, where one part in a hundred would have moved it eight times the run's own floor. Four fixed ratios of one quantity make the gain reductions a rank one table, whose columns would stand in one proportion; measured, that proportion walks from 1.682 to 1.523 across the four states, and the ratio each of the three returns changes with how far over the threshold it is asked.
whyNotNamed: A limiter is what the page calls it and what the readings are consistent with, and naming it would add nothing this claim does not already say. What would be worth naming -- the shape of the knee that makes three of the four states behave as they do -- is exactly what has not been read: three thresholds is not enough points to fit a knee to, and a name put on it now would be the part retracted first.
adds: Each record says what the level was at each setting of the threshold byte under one state of the ratio byte. What is read out of them here is what no one of them holds: that the four together are not four multipliers of one quantity. The scale of the threshold byte in decibels is read off the state that is linear in it, the other three are then held against that scale, and the departure is a comparison across four records. The ladder adds the second thing none of the sweeps can say, because the byte it would have to be said with has run out of range.
refutedBy: The state printed `1/100` ceasing to be straight in the threshold byte somewhere in its range, which would take away the axis every other figure here is held against. Or the decibels a step coming back different at another input level, which would say the byte is not a threshold. Or the constant the type takes off above the knee moving with the input, which would make it limiting rather than a loss.
whatItWouldChange: Two of the eight printed parameters of a type that carried no structural reading at all. A renderer given this type can put its threshold where the byte asks and knows that one of its four ratio settings is the printed number and that three of them are not -- which is the difference between approximating the stage and knowing which part of it is approximate.

eraPriors.claim: A stage of this period computes its gain from a level detector through a short table rather than from a logarithm, so a ratio exact in decibels is the expensive case and a ratio exact only far from the threshold is the ordinary one.
eraPriors.why: It says why three of four states might depart from a printed number in the same direction while the fourth does not: a state that clamps needs no ratio arithmetic at all and can be exact for free.
eraPriors.wouldBeWrongIf: One of the three departing states came back exact in decibels somewhere in its range while the clamping one did not. The prior is about which of the four is cheap to get right, and that ordering is the whole of it.

alternatives.reading: The four states are four fixed ratios and the departure from them is in the reading rather than in the unit.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: The repeats of one setting agree at the first order to 0.0 of a decibel, and the four states above the knee agree to 0.01. The departure is one and a half decibels, which is two orders larger than either. The whole order series moves together as well, so it is a gain that is being read and not a shape.

alternatives.reading: The threshold byte is not linear in decibels, and the three states curve because the axis they are read against does.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: The axis is read off the fourth state, whose gain reduction is straight in the byte over both stretches -- 0.4776 and 0.4767 decibels a step. A bent axis would bend that state too, and it is the state with the most of the axis in it.

alternatives.reading: The threshold byte does not move a threshold. It sets how much of the level over a fixed threshold is taken, so what looks like three states departing is the two bytes doing one job between them.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: The part's own volume was walked down thirty-six decibels at three settings of the threshold byte on each of two states of the ratio byte. This reading requires the three gain reduction curves of one state to be one curve times a constant, so that their quotient is one number at every input; measured on the arm printed `1/100` that quotient is 0.700, 0.657, 0.604, 0.531, 0.342, 0.003 and 0.006 down the ladder, where this reading needs 0.657 at all seven. Fitted as a vertical scale it leaves 1.70 to 3.05 decibels on the four comparisons; fitted as a sideways move it leaves 0.03 to 0.48, against eight rungs that repeat to 0.010. The move is also the same on both states of the ratio byte -- 9.96 against 9.95, and 20.09 against 20.09 -- which is what a quantity the ratio byte is not part of looks like.

alternatives.reading: The state printed `1/1.5` is a ratio like the other three, and what is a quarter away is the reading of it rather than the state.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: It is not. The ladder and the threshold sweep share no quantity -- one is the output against the level going in at a fixed byte, the other is gain reduction against the byte at a fixed level -- and the ladder returns 0.2499 where the sweep's chord converts to 0.2469. What the page prints against that state is 0.3333, which is five times the spread the other three states' fits show and twenty-five times what two independent readings of this one disagree by.

alternatives.reading: The four states are the page's table with two of its four entries wrong, rather than four even quarter steps of one quantity.

separatedBy.observable: Nothing this unit's output can be asked. The two readings return the same four numbers.

predicts.four even quarter steps: a quarter, a half, three quarters, all
predicts.the page's table with two entries wrong: a quarter, a half, three quarters, all

separatedBy.sensitivity_here: The ladder routed past the effect repeats to 0.010 of a decibel across the run's eight directories, and it bounds nothing here: the two readings do not differ in any quantity, so no floor applies to the difference.
separatedBy.why_not_separable: They return the same four numbers. Even quarter steps of one quantity and the page's table with two of its four entries wrong both give a quarter, a half, three quarters and all, because the middle two entries are printed as a half and a quarter already. Nothing that comes out of this unit distinguishes a byte indexing four even fractions from a byte indexing a table that happens to hold them, which is the same shape the level class parked for the same reason. What argues for the steps is the era and not a measurement -- two bits and one multiply against a four entry table -- and a prior may carry a claim and may not close one.
